# The Role of the Epigenome in Translating Neighborhood Disadvantage Into Health Disparities

Kenneth Olden1 & Heather A. Olden2 & Yu-Sheng Lin1

Published online: 9 April 2015 # Springer International Publishing AG (outside the USA) 2015

Abstract The possible causal role of the environment in health disparities is not well understood, even though it has been a national priority for many years. Progress to investigate the relationship between genetics, environmental exposures, and health outcomes has been hampered by the lack of analytical tools to quantify the combined or cumulative effect of multiple chemical and non-chemical stressors on gene expression. The studies cited here provide a strong rationale for using epigenomic analysis to assess cumulative risk from multiple environmental exposures over the life course. The environment-specific Bimprints^ on the genome, coupled with transcriptomics and metabolomics, can be used to advance our understanding of the relationship between neighborhood disadvantage and health disparities.

Keywords Epigenetics . Epigenome . Genetic . DNA methylation . Environmental health . Health disparities

Introduction

Recent advances in cell and molecular biology have greatly enhanced our ability to elucidate the role of the environment in the etiology of common non-communicable diseases (e.g.,

cancer, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease). Over the past decades, the so-called revolution in genomics has transformed our understanding of the role of environmental stressors in the development of complex phenotypes. Contrary to our original expectation, we now know that genes do not determine biological fate; they establish a range of possible phenotypic outcomes through complex interaction with the environment. A second unexpected finding is that gene expression is regulated by both genetic (e.g., DNA nucleotide sequence) and epigenetic mechanisms. To date, the three best known epigenetic mechanisms, collectively part of the epigenome, include DNA methylation, chemical modification of the histone component of chromatin, and alteration in the expression of short non-coding RNAs (e.g., miRNAs). These potentially durable and environmentspecific modifications provide a plausible mechanism to explain how differential exposures associated with living in a disadvantaged neighborhood can become biologically embedded, with long-lasting and even possibly transgenerational effects on human health. This new era of science has a great potential to fundamentally change our understanding of the causes of significant common diseases.

Neighborhood Context Matters

Exactly why neighborhood or environmental context matters for human health and disease remains largely unknown. To date, the design of studies is less well suited to address this question because the appropriate tools have not been available. To increase our understanding of how neighborhood influences human health, one must expand the concept of the environment to include both chemical and non-chemical stressors. That is, environmental exposures need to be considered in the context of the community or social environment in which people actually live. Although researchers acknowledge that neighborhood-associated differences in health outcomes may have multiple determinants, most efforts still concentrate on the investigation of single risk factors.

The risk assessment practice typically focuses on one hazardous substance at a time and on one or a small number of health endpoints, and does not take into consideration the cumulative or combined impact of exposure to multiple chemical and non-chemical stressors over the life course. Of note, even though the health risk caused by a single stressor may be small, the public health consequences of cumulative exposure to multiple risk factors can be substantial in the population. Therefore, there is a need to assess the effects of cumulative or combined exposure to multiple environmental stressors and this requires the development of tools to integrate community characteristics into the risk assessment-risk management paradigm. For example, it has been suggested that epigenetic modifications can theoretically represent every chemical and non-chemical stressor to which populations are exposed from conception to death [1•, 2•]. This includes endogenous (e.g., hormones or oxygen radicals) and exogenous (e.g., diet, stress, air pollutants) agents. It has been repeatedly observed that environment-induced epigenetic influence persists even after the stressors have long gone. This observation suggests that signatures or profiles of DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNAs can serve as a long-term biomarker of past exposures, providing a powerful approach to examine the relationship between neighborhood context and health outcome [2•]. By combining epigenetic signatures with other B-omic^ technologies including transcriptomics and metabolomics, one can identify metabolic pathways affected by neighborhood disadvantage.

Health Disparities and Socioeconomic Position

Health disparities remain a significant public health problem in the United States. As compared to whites, African Americans have 1.3-fold higher risk of dying from coronary disease, 1.8-fold higher for diabetes, and 2-fold higher for hypertension [3, 4]. Environmental justice advocates and researchers have long maintained that this increased prevalence of morbidity and shorter life expectancy among racial minority groups and socioeconomically Bdisadvantaged^ versus Badvantaged^ populations are due to disproportionate exposure to environmental hazards [5, 6]. In fact, studies confirm that environmental risks are not uniformly distributed among the U.S. populations [7, 8]. Minority, the elderly, and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities are often disproportionately exposed to higher levels of hazardous environmental chemicals [9•]. These so-called Bhigh-end^ exposures represent levels of exposures that the general population does not encounter. Furthermore, these outliers are not captured in traditional risk management practices. Whereas the exact causes of health disparities are unknown, they are likely due to multiple risk factors associated with poverty, including differences in access to health care and

healthy foods, mental stress related to neighborhood violence, exposure to higher levels of environmental pollutants, and unhealthy behaviors [10]. Genetic variation could also play a role. However, there is very little evidence to support this view and several findings are not supportive of a significant causal role for genetics [11]. In contrast, numerous studies support the view of the disproportionate exposure to multiple extrinsic factors in Bdisadvantage^ neighborhoods. For example, air pollution studies comparing inner city neighborhoods found that there is significant variability due to traffic patterns and siting of bus depots, incinerators, and manufacturing facilities. Socioeconomically disadvantaged communities in New York City were often disproportionately exposed to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and particulates [12–14]. For example, six bus depots are located in Harlem and Washington Heights, predominantly African American and Hispanic communities. Similarly, smoking, malnutrition, and pesticide use are also more prevalent in these neighborhoods [15]. When comparing the three neighborhoods in New York City reported to have the worst health status with the three neighborhoods with the best health status (Fig. 1), sociodemographics (Fig. 1a) such as poverty and minority status were strongly associated with the worst health outcomes (Fig. 1b). Studies are underway in our laboratory to test our prediction that the epigenome of populations with such disparate health outcomes may have been uniquely programmed by neighborhood exposures (depicted schematically in Fig. 2). As such, one can use neighborhood profiles to identify gene pathways responsible for poor health outcomes of populations exposed to neighborhood disadvantage. The ability to identify neighborhoods at increased risk for developing common diseases, related to varied socioeconomic status (SES) and environmental exposures, is a public health priority.

Epigenome as a Biomarker for Cumulative Risk

Over the past 20 years, there has been a dramatically increasing interest in neighborhood effects on health [16]. In this paper, we further elaborate on our earlier hypothesis about how neighborhood environmental exposures interact with intrinsic biological factors (e.g., genes, age, and gender) to influence health outcomes [2•]. According to our model, advantaged and disadvantaged neighborhoods differentially Bimprint^ the epigenome, and these durable modifications can be detected as an exposure signature. These environment-induced epigenetic modifications can be used as a biomarker in epidemiologic studies to assess the cumulative impact of lifetime exposures to multiple chemical and non-chemical stressors. Numerous findings are consistent with this hypothesis in that they have shown that exposure to chemical, social and behavioral factors leave their imprint on the epigenome [1•]. For example, aberrant DNA methylation, histone modifications, or altered expression of short non-coding RNAs can be induced by a variety of environmental agents, including

Furthermore, most if not all, diseases are associated with epigenetic changes, many of which alter gene expression and susceptibility to disease. Case control studies have shown that epigenetic profiles, obtained using tissue from peripheral blood, can be used to distinguish between healthy controls and individuals with various disease phenotypes [17–19]. It is well established that a link exists between nutrition status, critical periods of development, disease pathogenesis, and epigenetic modifications [29]. Dietary restriction during pregnancy reduces methylation of the promoter of the glucocorticoid receptor genes involved in hormone-induced stress response and hypertension, with increase in expression of the glucocorticoid receptor. Food deprivation during pregnancy also resulted in low birthweight babies that were at high risk for development of type 2 diabetes and coronary heart disease in adulthood [30]. The effects of food deprivation was transgenerational in that grandchildren of the same gender as the in utero exposed individuals had increased risk for multiple diseases [31]. In summary, multiple human studies have confirmed that epigenetic programming can occur during both adulthood and embryonic development [32]. Such studies provide a mechanistic basis for the Barker hypothesis that adult diseases have their origins during embryonic development [33]. Despite improvements in the quality of the air since the passage of the Clean Air Act in 1963, adverse health effects from exposure to air pollutants, such as ozone, particulate material, PAHs, lead, and NO2 are still common occurrences. It has been estimated that air pollution contributes about 6 % of total human mortality [34]. Numerous studies have shown that exposure to high levels of air pollutants increase rates of hospital admissions and deaths from lung and cardiovascular related disorders, and that asthma prevalence was most consistently associated with socioeconomic status. Exposure to air pollutants is also associated with epigenome modification. For example, diesel exhaust particulates altered the expression of short non-coding RNAs and histones in human airway epithelial cells; and network analysis of the 12 most altered short non-coding RNAs showed that they were part of the inflammatory response pathway associated with disease pathogenesis [35–37]. Exposure to PAHs and PM2.5 have modest effects on the global methylation of the promoter sequences of genes involved in cancer, cardiovascular, and respiratory diseases [38]. Exposure to air pollution is also associated with hypermethylation of candidate genes that play a role in the pathogenesis of asthma (e.g., the transcription factor interferon gamma) [39, 40]. Remarkable progress in epigenomic technologies has been made recently in identifying possible interactive events among exposure to air pollutants, development of cardiovascular and pulmonary dysfunctions, and epigenetic modifications. For example, both acute and chronic exposure to metal-rich PM2.5 were shown to be associated with increased risk for cardiovascular anomalies, such as variation in heart rate, systematic inflammation, and alterations in DNA methylation levels in Alu retrotransposons and long interspersed nuclear elements 1 (LINE-1) [41]. While the mechanisms by which Alu and LINE-1 methylation levels cause cardiovascular effects are largely unclear, a possible mechanism is the

generation of reactive oxygen species. Exposure to PM2.5 can also induce oxidative damage to DNA and inhibit interaction between DNA and methyltransferase. Ambient air pollutants have also been shown to affect the methylation levels of genes involved in inflammation and oxidative stress [42]. Studies by Breton et al. [38, 43] showed that exposure to PM2.5 altered the methylation of several genes in the nitric oxide synthase (NOS) pathway, suggesting that these particulates may alter the production of nitric oxide. Nitric oxide homeostasis plays an important role in modulation of airway vascular smooth muscle and inflammation and therefore altered NOS expression may adversely affect lung function. To better understand how multiple pathways potentially are involved in the pathogenesis of cardiovascular disease, Bind et al. [44] developed a novel pathway analysis approach to determine whether genetic polymorphisms within relevant pathways modified the association with exposure to particulate air pollution and expression of pathway-specific biomarkers. They observed a significant association between air pollution and expression of biomarkers (e.g., C-reactive protein, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, and vascular cell adhesion molecule-1) of these pathways and that the association was influenced by the genetic background. Also, the effects of time pattern (short and intermediate term) on biomarker expression was exposure specific [44, 45].

Conclusion

Despite substantial improvements in health care and environmental health protection over the past 50 years, large disparities in health persist in the U.S. population. Socioeconomically disadvantaged groups and minority populations (e.g., African Americans and Hispanics) tend to have worse health outcomes, with respect to higher rates of disease and reduced life expectancy, compared to the overall population in the U.S. [46, 47]. A more recent countybased survey of the U.S. population found that disparities in life expectancy can be as much as 15 years in communities that are experiencing severe poverty [8]. Most distressing is the likelihood that such devastating disparities will increase as poverty grows, and African American and Hispanic populations become a significantly larger fraction of the U.S. population. Also, the epidemic of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease among these vulnerable populations may further increase because of the transgenerational effects of epigenetic modifications. The legacy of multiple generations of exposure to higher levels of environmental stressors is likely Bembedded^ in the epigenome.

The premise that environmental health risks are borne disproportionately by socioeconomically disadvantaged communities has gained wider acceptance over the past 25 years [48, 49]. However, slow progress in understanding the relationship between neighborhood disadvantage and health disparities may be in part due to the lack of methodological tools to evaluate the cumulative effect of multiple environmental stressors on genetic substrates. The studies cited above provide a strong rationale to consider the link between epigenetic modifications and health disparities, with the epigenome serving as a biosensor of combined or cumulative exposure to diverse and multiple stressors over the life course. The facts that epigenetic changes are durable and often precede disease pathology make them useful as diagnostic indicators. Our prediction is that there are disease- and exposure-specific signatures or profiles with respect to DNA methylation, histone modifications, and expression of non-coding RNAs. In combination with transcriptomics and metabolomics, one can further gain an improved understanding of gene networks and metabolic pathways affected by the epigenetic modifications. However, not every modification will lead to altered gene expression; like single nucleotide polymorphisms, some will not have functional consequences. Another interesting feature of the epigenome is that the epigenetic modifications are reversible; Bdurable does not mean permanent^. Unlike mutations, which alter the nucleotide sequence of DNA, the structures and mechanisms altered in the epigenome are still intact and therefore, can potentially be reversed by environmental amelioration, and by social or pharmacologic intervention. The most active and successful area of investigation involves the development of inhibitors to block histone deacetylation and DNA methylation in the treatment of cancer [50]. Moreover, some success has been achieved by changing the neighborhood environment. For example, as shown in a randomized study conducted by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, the health status of children considerably improved when moving from a high poverty neighborhood to a higher income neighborhood [51].

Boundaries of Form and Subject in Fifteenth-Century dits

Helen Swift

University of Oxford

There is significant continuity in the late-medieval dit, the most popular form of first-

person narrative courtly poetry in French. There are also, however, certain 15th century

developments that raise in new ways important questions about boundaries of selfhood and self-

definition in the dit: what constitutes the borders of a first-person subject? What are the

parameters of “narrative” as an operable category in relation to “lyric” and “discursive”? These

developments lie in “arguably the most significant courtly poetic phenomenon in the fifteenth

century” (Hult 779): Alain Chartier’s Belle Dame sans Mercy (1424, BDSM), the poetic debate

that it generated over the next half-century, and the legacy of Chartier’s influence attested by

continued reception of the querelle into early print (Bouchet, “A Good Carter as Guide”).

BDSM generates three first-person subjects through its scenario of overheard debate: the

lover, the lady, and the narrator. All three are elaborated in literary responses to the poem, with

slippages between lover and narrator being developed in ways that promote malleable

boundaries of subject-hood so as to offer fresh perspectives on the courtly love situation (Swift

91-120). I consider three responses – Achille Caulier’s La Cruelle femme en amour (1430), and

two anonymous dits: Le Debat sans conclusion (before 1460), and Le Purgatoire d’amours

(1463) – which feature together in the first anthology of dits and lyrics to appear in print in

France, Le Jardin de plaisance et fleur de rethorique (1501, JdP). Anthologisation introduces

further boundary negotiation: framing intertextuality as material interaction through co-textual

juxtaposition and rubrication; embedding individual dits in overarching adumbrated narrative

and discursive frameworks; and, in the case of JdP, collating as a single item several rondeaux

This chapter’s group of related texts thus interrogates in a quite particular way the

Relational identity in BDSM

BDSM stages a voluble, self-styled amant martir suitor (l’Amant) being rejected by an

allegedly merciless, rhetorically adroit lady (la Dame) in a debate of some seventy-two

octosyllabic huitains, overheard through a trellis by a narrator (l’Acteur) whose twenty-eight

stanzas book-end the poem with self-presentation, observation, and commentary. It is important

not to diminish retrospectively the complexity of Chartier’s original poem: scholarship on the

querelle frequently notes that the responses “develop increasingly elaborate narrative settings”

(Armstrong and Kay 143); whilst it is true that the narrative content of BDSM is quite simple,

its narratorial self-presentation and discursive positioning are as sophisticated as any of the later

contributions. L’Acteur introduces himself in terms of superlative singularity as a bereaved

lover, “le plus doulent des amoureux” (4: “the saddest of lovers”);1 having asserted a declining

amorous identity, he then depicts an unraveling writerly identity (“[…] il fault que je cesse / De

ditter…”, [9-10: “[…] I must stop / the writing”]) accompanied by embodied dislocation and

impotence affecting “langue,” “bouche,” “yeulx,” “cuer” (20-23: “tongue, mouth, eyes, heart”).

In testamentary vein, presenting himself as left-over and discomposed (“[La Mort] me laisse

seul,” [7: “[Death] left me alone”]), he leaves to others the possibility of composition (“Je laisse

[…] / Faire chançons, dis, et balades,” [25, 27: “I leave […] / to write and sing songs and

situating himself in relation to them; and the “himself” that he delineates is not itself a pre-

Subjective judgment is key to the querelle: of the twenty or so responses to BDSM that

accrue by 1440, the majority of the most narratively and discursively developed texts adopt a

courtroom fiction to try and re-try la Dame’s alleged culpability for murder. They offer

“selective judicialized re-readings” (Bouchet 330) of the poem which, whilst cultivating

through their legal apparatus an expectation of dispassionate forensic analysis, in fact

underscore the absence of any objective measure of truth, most virtuosically in Achille Caulier’s

La Cruelle femme en amours (CF). Personified Verité, a barrister, is called upon to account for

having supported la Dame’s cause (as occurred in the anonymous “Dame lealle en amours”

(1426-30)), and alleges a remarkable twist of illegitimate impersonation:

Celle qui se mist en mon nom

Pour ceste cause soustenir

Ne fut aultre que Fiction.

Poëterie lui fist venir

Et ma semblable devenir (CF, 329-33)

[“The one who presented herself in my name / in order to defend the lady’s case / was

none other than Fiction, conjured up by Poetry, to appear in my image”]

In a moment of consummate metafictional maneuvering, Caulier evokes the nature of

subjecthood in the querelle: identity is not a given; it is subject to constant mutation (“se

transmüa,” [334: “transfigured”]), construction and recomposition. It is only ever a subjective

judgment, by the person perceiving themselves or by an “aultre” who perceives them: for

example, there is no “belle dame sans mercy” prior to l’Acteur’s gesture of bringing into being

through naming in BDSM, and that naming remains an allegation, a challengeable judgment

call. Hence the potential for endless propagation of debate.

Caulier manifests a particular predilection for disrupting boundaries in his two querelle

experienced by l’Acteur strikes something of a keynote: he encounters a metamorphic palace

divers” (CF 127-8: “and each figure metamorphosed / from one form to another and back

again”). This vision represents the tensions of subjecthood suspended in formation between one

single figure: “n’y pos mon regard arrester / Sur une chose […]” (118-19: “I could not fix my

eye / on a single thing […]”). Such a relational, mutational principle is applied by Caulier in

on the love debate. OA opens unlike many other responses: its Acteur is not melancholic, but is

approaches the lady to whom he is devoted and boldly discloses his ardor, which she rejects;

he persists, but eventually loses hope in the face of reiterated refusals. Grief-stricken, he

surrenders himself to being an amant martir, and then has a dream vision which embarks him

on the journey to the hospital of Love that constitutes the main body of the poem. OA’s Acteur

approached the Dame, prior to BDSM’s debate, such that OA’s opening offers the “backstory”

mutational maneuver, not least in reducing the history of the affair from seventy-two stanzas of

structures the narrative, and, through homophony, the “serf” (“servant”) who is l’Amant being

initiated into love’s service by Cupid’s officers. DSC raises at least two further answers: la

Dame and the reader. In the copies in which DSC features as a discrete item, and thus does not

need to elaborate a continuing hunt narrative, a summary conclusion is imposed on the chase:

“Illec fut la beste tenue / Et prinse a force devenue” (fol. 152v: “there was the animal captured

/ and taken by force”). Designating the captured quarry “la beste” evokes a number of potential

referents: the deer itself, of course, but also, metaphorically, the desiring Amant – is he caught

15

in the snares of his own melancholic devotion? La Dame deploys hunting metaphors in the

course of their debate, advising him, “vos fillez autre part tendez” (fol. 150r: “cast your nets

elsewhere”) and declaring “oncques es latz d’amours n’entray” (fol. 152v: “I shall never enter

the snares of love”); she thus seems to preclude herself from capture, but the grammatical

femininity of “la beste” offers the possibility of her having nonetheless been taken by force,

against her will. Or is love itself – labeled in DSC’s woodcut illustration in JdP – ensnared,

which we as audience are tracking through the text and its co-texts? JdP’s rudimentary narrative

framework outlines a wander through a garden wherein several tales entertain a coursing

situation, such as “une chasse appellee la pipee au dieu d’amours” (fol. 187v: “a course called

the hunt of the god of Love”). Are we as readers the hunters, watching for hermeneutic traps?

We recall, for instance, the use of a hunting metaphor to depict the activity of judges in BDSM:

“leurs juges […] / Qui les tiennent en leurs liens” (79-80: “their judges, […] who held them in

thrall”). What might ensnare our understanding?

Identity formation through “ung autre”

DSC’s Dame supports her case for refusing Amant’s advances through allusive

reference to unhappy precedents: “J’ay bien des autres souvenir / Qui ont perdu honneur et

gloires” (fol. 152r: “I have a clear memory of others / who have lost honour and glory”). But

she names none, which is highly unusual for querelle debates, and for late-medieval dits more

generally, often awash with enumerated exempla from an array of sources: biblical, Classical

and contemporary; mythological, legendary and historical. Such citational practice plays an

important role in first-person identity formation: from the speaker’s perspective, it is part of

their self-fashioning, defining themselves in relation to cases that stand as models, such as Echo,

Thisbe, or Dido as tragic victims of love; from the implied authorial perspective, it offers the

possibility for character critique, with the reader invited to assess how appropriately or

rhetorically successfully the speaker shapes their self-presentation, as in Machaut’s JRN


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

(Blumenfeld-Kosinski 142). Chartier’s Dame and Amant themselves become mythemes,

commonplaces of contemporary mythography, like the protagonists of the 13th century

Chastelaine de Vergy.

Le Purgatoire d’amours (PA), a late querelle contribution attributed to Pierre Michault

and dated in manuscript copies to 1463, dramatizes the construction of a lover’s identity. Before

Cupid’s court, its Amant requests the return of his heart, casting himself as an amant martir and

supporting his case with over twenty exemplary lovers tormented by “les dons d’amours […] /

Jusques a la mort” (JdP, fol. 185v: “the gifts of love […] / until their death”), from Old

Testament Sarah to the Amants of both BDSM and OA. Exceptionally, in the context of querelle

juridical dramas, he gets to plead his case himself rather than being represented posthumously

by others. The verdict does not, however, fall in his favor: Cupid concludes that he is an

impudent, impatient servant, and thus not a “vray amant” (fol. 185r: “true lover”), akin to CA’s

Amant Oultrecuydé, though PA’s Acteur aligns him more to l’Amant Parfait: “si suis certain

que cest amant est pur” (fol. 187r: “I am certain that this lover is pure”). PA’s Amant is

disciplined by three days of punishment in purgatory. Cupid thereby metes out a corrective

lesson that, retrospectively, could have saved BDSM’s Amant from his obstinate pursuit of the

Belle Dame and thereby changed the whole course of the querelle.

L’Amant’s self-defense is offered for our critical consideration: the dreaming Acteur

who witnesses the courtroom scene notes prefatorily that “il par sa parole / Monstra assez qu’il

venoit de l’escolle” (fol. 184r: “he by his speech / demonstrated amply that he came from [that]

school”); we recall DSC’s Dame’s caution that this itself may be reason for skeptical scrutiny.

Amant introduces his argumentative method: “Vray compteray ou les histoires mentent / Car

ja du mien n’y mettray quelque chose” (fol. 185r-185v: “I shall tell the truth where the stories

lie / since I shall not add in anything of my own”). From his point of view, the chiastically

emphasized antithesis underscores the truth value of exempla which he posits as objective and

univocal; for the reader, such a categorical distinction and proclaimed elimination of


<!-- Page 17 -->


17

subjectivity sound a warning bell signaling the speaker’s discursive and narratorial ignorance.

Argument and storytelling have no impersonal truth, as was demonstrated earlier on in PA when

l’Amant first presented his case: it was initially received by President Loyaulté who, on seeking

colleagues’ counsel, “a fin de mieulx la verité scavoir” (fol.183v: “in order better to know the

truth”), received multiple, irreconcilable views: “la diversité / D’oppinions et divers jugemens”

(fol. 183v: “the diversity / of opinions and conflicting judgments”); at a loss how to resolve

them, he deferred upwards to Cupid.

The necessary selectivity in l’Amant’s catalogue of exempla already manifests “du mien

[…] quelque chose” (fol. 185v: “something of my own”), and not always competently – for

instance, confusedly presenting Echo and Narcissus as equal victims. He also imposes

subjective interpretation in his enlistment of BDSM:

L’amant priant la dame sans mercy

Finablement mourut en desespoir.

Ung autre fut prouchain de mort aussi

Ayant le cueur de mesme mercy

Quant il trouva en l’ospital espoir. (PA, fol. 186r)

[“The lover who implored the merciless lady / ultimately died in despair. / Another was

also close to death, / with a heart similarly [seeking] mercy / when he found hope in the

hospital”]

Predictably for a “languissant douloureux” (fol. 184r: “languishing wretch”), he presents

the death of Chartier’s Amant as established fact, and aligns him with Caulier’s to construct a

succession of amant martir antecedents in contemporary culture. The designation “ung autre”

is repeated to introduce each new analog, rendering the referents allusive and soliciting

audience interpretation to identify them, such as “ung aultre amoureux” (“another lover”):

Par [amour morte] a vostre occasion

Il monstra bien qu’il estoit douloureux

18

Quant il vous dist tant de motz rigoreux (fol. 186r )

[“dying for love by your doing, / he truly showed that he was wretched / when he spoke

to you so many harsh words”].

Is this intended to designate an individual case? Is an intertextually alert audience

invited to propose likely candidates, such as the speaker of Chartier’s Complainte (“Las! Or

n’ay plus ce que j’avoye, Amors,” [22: “Alas! Now I no longer have what I had, Love”])? On

the one hand, Amant’s slip into allusiveness seems contrary to his objective of unequivocal

enumeration, and thus a point of discursive weakness; on the other, the plurality of possible

referents across the corpus of medieval dits serves to accrete an ever-expanding body of

examples to buttress his argument. Viewed metatextually, his “ung autre” method draws

attention to the intertextual relationality of typified dit-lover identity: whilst it marks a shift

from one distinct case to another, it nevertheless points to the continuity linking them together

as a chain of related cases, suggesting an approach to the boundaries of subjecthood privileging

permeability and mutation, not discrete distinction.

The richest reading of PA is afforded, as it was for DSC, by examination in its material

context, which in early print transmission likewise includes JdP: “Comment au jardin de

plaisance l’amoureux est au purgatoire d’amours et privé de joye” (fol. 182v: “How, in the

pleasure garden, the lover is in the purgatory of love and deprived of happiness”). JdP’s

anthologisation of courtly love poetry offers particular, cross-textual candidates for PA’s

“autres,” most especially with reference to the series of amant martir items at the volume’s

close, including George Chastelain’s Oultré d’amours (before 1450), Pierre de Hauteville’s La

Confession et testament de l’amant trespassé de dueil (1441-47), concluded by an anonymous

Epitaphe dedicated, with similar allusiveness, to “l’oultré d’amour pour amour morte” (fol.

258v: “the one overcome by love who died for love”). The poems’ title-rubrics foster

interconnection: de Hauteville’s Confession’s picks up Chastelain’s Oultré’s protagonist,

“Comment le chevalier oultré d’amours trespasse de dueil de sa dame” (fol. 247r: “How the

knight overcome by love dies of grief for his lady”), who is then carried through into the

Epitaphe’s text, adumbrating progression from life to death, but in sketchy, gestural terms,

passing through, in each fiction, a specific discursive and narrative situation.

Their inclusion in JdP opens up cross-textual resonances for both DSC and PA. In both,

a speaker evokes the arc of an amant martir’s trajectory that one could see to be traced across

the volume: DSC’s Dame advises l’Amant:

Car l’amour de quoy vous usez

Est de fol commencement

Et de si triste finement (fol. 152r)

[“the love that you practise / has a foolish beginning / and a very sad ending”];

and Cupid counsels PA’s Amant: “Et pour brief, oncques amant, tant fust fin, / Ne me

servit sans doloreuse fin” (fol. 185r: “in sum, no lover, however shrewd, / ever served me

without a wretched end”). The “oultree [or ‘oultrecudyee’?] folie” (fol. 152r: “overwhelming

[or ‘overweaning’?] foolishness”) of DSC’s Amant anticipates “l’oultré d’amours” (fol. 258v:

“the one overcome by love”) of the anthology’s close, whose demise fulfils PA’s promise of

“doloreuse fin”. Paratextually, the title-rubrics promote narrative movement both spatially,

around the putative garden, and temporally, through the lover’s amorous experience and

decline; they outline, therefore, ‘le mouvement biographique de la compilation’ (Frieden, “Le

Jardin de plaisance”), but the nature of that biographical movement needs careful

understanding – it is not purely linear, given, for instance, how DSC’s lexically prominent

“infortuné” resonates with the figure designated as the author of JdP’s opening versification

treatise: “l’infortuné” (fol. A2v: “the ill-fated”); nor is it exclusive to a single figure, but, like

DSC’s Dame’s affections, is inclusive of each “autre” together in a collective coherence:

“chascun et vous aussi” (“everyone, including you”).

Whilst there is no individuality of identity, there is nonetheless specificity in the

discursive situation of each text, as indexed by the other organizing paratextual feature of JdP,

its woodcuts. Each offers “une contextualisation énonciative immédiate” (Buron 222) of the

poem it prefaces, but direct ontological representation does not individualise. The generic

nature of each human embodiment of “l’Acteur,” “le chevalier,” “le prisoner,” or “l’Amant,”

labeled to identify the particular type concerned (with those types nonetheless being porous and

not mutually exclusive), instantiates the principle of each “autre amoureux” of courtly love

narrative. Like DSC’s Amant’s self-presentation as superlatively cursed, “infortuné / […] /

Suis-je devant tout homme né,” the first-person lover defines himself as set apart from everyone

else, and at the same time cannot define himself except with reference to everyone else, hence

my privileging of relationality as the key concept for understanding subjectivities in formation

in late-medieval dits.

Boundaries of form in JdP

JdP compiles narrative and lyric poetry. As I noted above in respect of the jeu-parti

moment in DSC’s debate, and the interpenetration between Chartier’s Complainte and BDSM,

the boundary between these forms is not fixed. A particular case in point is an item in-between

DSC and PA, entitled “La complainte du prisonnier d’amours faicte au jardin de plaisance” (fol.

161r: “The lament of the prisoner of love made in the pleasure garden”), which comprises

fourteen rondeaux by Chartier presented each as a stanza of the composite complaint. Each

voices a disconsolate love lament, with the title-rubric perhaps deriving from the opening of the

third rondeau/stanza: “Au povre prisonnier, ma dame” (fol. 161r: “to this poor prisoner, my

lady”). Recalling l’Amant’s predicament in DSC, they express a typically lyric stuck-ness, an

inability to move forward narratively, and instead cycle discursively around the same

oxymoronic state: “Je n’ay povoir de vivre en joye / Et si ne puis mourir de dueil” (fol. 161v:

“I cannot live in happiness / and I cannot die of grief”). A peculiarity of JdP is its double table

of contents at the end of the anthology: the first, of (mostly) narrative items that lists the title-

rubrics in chronological order through the volume; the second, which indexes individual lyrics


<!-- Page 21 -->


21

alphabetically by first line, form by form (ballades, rondeaux, chansons, etc.). “La complainte”

features in the former, which prompts us to consider the extent to which there is any meaningful

distinction between the first-person lover-speaker of lyric and narrative items when the self-

fashioning of that persona is as an amant martir. Dying, of course, marks progression, but the

transition itself is never experienced narratively: it is only ever discursively anticipated (and

then, most often, like the favor desired of the beloved, as a longed-for but feared, unknowable

outcome – “Ou mon desir s’assouvira / Ou ma tristesse m’occira,” fol. 161r: “Either my desire

will overwhelm me / or my sorrow will kill me”) or recalled in lamentation by a third party, as

in the Epitaphe for “l’oultré d’amours pour amour morte.”

One distinguishing textual feature of narrative items is the presence of an Acteur, whose

work of framing the tale may be narrative and/or discursive, and may, in the author’s interests

of generating debate about the debate staged within a poem, be deployed to prompt disjuncture

rather than coherence, such as dispensing judgment that sits at odds with events or character

presentation, like PA’s conviction that its punished Amant is a true lover. L’Acteur does not,

therefore, figure the extratextual audience’s point of view: they position themselves at one

remove from his “je”: overhearing him eavesdropping, witnessing him spying. Articulation of

the overall story, that which includes all the first-persons of a given tale and, in an anthology,

interrelation with its cross-textual “autres,” requires the extratextual audience as “relateur”:

without them, the debate is “sans relacion”; it is always, and most productively, “sans

conclusion.”
